For $n\ge0$ and $a,x\in\{0,1\}^{n}$, define the one-bit **binary dot product**
$$
a\cdot x:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}(a_i\land x_i),
$$
where $\land$ is Boolean conjunction and $\bigoplus$ is the left-to-right fold of XOR, with empty fold $0$. It is the parity of the number of coordinates where both bits are $1$. Under the quotient operations of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]], this bit represents the sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}[a_i]_2[x_i]_2$ in $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$; the equality uses only the operation definitions, not the field axioms.

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

For $n\ge0$ and a binary word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^n$, define its
**big-endian index**

$$\operatorname{enc}_n(x):=\sum_{k<n}x_k\,2^{\,n-1-k}.$$

Thus the first wire is the most significant bit. For $n=0$, the domain
$\{0,1\}^0$ consists only of the empty word $()$, and the empty sum gives
$\operatorname{enc}_0(())=0$. In an ordered $n$-qubit
computational basis, the word $x$ occupies the slot numbered
$\operatorname{enc}_n(x)$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

derivations.claim: By [F1], $(-1)^{x\cdot z}=\prod_{i<n}(-1)^{x_i z_i}$, since the exponent parity is the sum of the coordinate products modulo two. Distributivity over the finite Cartesian product gives $\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}(-1)^{x\cdot z}=\prod_{i<n}\left(1+(-1)^{z_i}\right).$ Each factor is $2$ when $z_i=0$ and $0$ when $z_i=1$. Thus the product is $2^n$ when all coordinates of $z$ vanish and is $0$ otherwise.

By [F2], on each factor $H|x_i\rangle=2^{-1/2}\sum_{y_i\in\{0,1\}}(-1)^{x_i y_i}|y_i\rangle$. Applying [F5] to the ordered product basis [F3] gives a coefficient $2^{-n/2}\prod_{i<n}(-1)^{x_i y_i}=2^{-n/2}(-1)^{x\cdot y}$ at $|y\rangle$, by [F1]. Summing these coefficients proves the tensor-Hadamard formula in the Statement.

A **decision task** is a root promise pair $(Y,N)$ of disjoint subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$, as in [[def-promise-problem]]: its promise domain is $Y\cup N$, and the required output is yes on $Y$ and no on $N$. No correctness condition is imposed outside that promise.

A **search task** is a pair $(D,R)$ where $D\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ is the promise domain and $R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\{0,1\}^*$ is a witness relation. On each $z\in D$, a correct solver must output a binary string $w$ with $(z,w)\in R$. It has no output obligation for $z\notin D$. Unlike a decision task, a search task need not divide its promise into yes and no sets.

For either task, an input encoding and input-length convention are specified separately; correctness is required only for encoded inputs in the declared promise.

For each encoded promised instance $z\in P_n$ of length $n$ (with $P_n$ as in [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]] and its task promise as in [[def-qa-task-and-promise-domain]]), a **query instance** specifies nonnegative integer widths $a(n),b(n)$ and a total function
$$
f_z:\{0,1\}^{a(n)}\to\{0,1\}^{b(n)}.
$$
The promise restricts which $z$ are legal; it does not restrict the address domain of $f_z$. Bit strings label the big-endian computational basis: for a word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1})$, its slot is $\sum_{k<r}x_k2^{r-1-k}$, with the empty word in slot $0$ ([[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]). Ket and bra notation uses the root convention $\langle x|y\rangle_D=\langle y,x\rangle_{\rm root}$ ([[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]). Its standard quantum query is the coherent XOR oracle from [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]], acting on those ordered register bases:
$$
U_{f_z}|x\rangle|y\rangle=|x\rangle|y\oplus f_z(x)\rangle,
$$
where $\oplus$ is coordinatewise addition modulo two, $x$ is an $a(n)$-bit address, and $y$ is a $b(n)$-bit target. One invocation is one query, regardless of the output width. A supplied matrix or a classical description of $f_z$ does not itself supply a circuit decomposition, state preparation, or controlled access at zero cost.

The access contract must specify whether controlled calls are supplied: a controlled call is the explicitly granted block operation $\operatorname{diag}(I,U)$ ([[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]) and does not follow from an ordinary black-box call. For this standard XOR oracle, $U_{f_z}^{\dagger}=U_{f_z}$ by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]], so an inverse query is the same operation as one ordinary query. Inverse access to any other unitary operation has its own explicitly declared availability and charge ([[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]]). An explicit matrix or classical description supplies no free circuit implementation, preparation, or data loading; those costs are recorded under the declared circuit and gate resource coordinates ([[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]], [[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

For every $n\ge0$, the map
$\operatorname{enc}_n:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,\ldots,2^n-1\}$ of
[[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]] is a bijection. Any permutation of the
$n$ bit positions therefore induces a permutation of the corresponding
computational basis.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of [[def-nat-order]] identified with
membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

A **decision task** is a root promise pair $(Y,N)$ of disjoint subsets of $\{0,1\}^*$, as in [[def-promise-problem]]: its promise domain is $Y\cup N$, and the required output is yes on $Y$ and no on $N$. No correctness condition is imposed outside that promise.

A **search task** is a pair $(D,R)$ where $D\subseteq\{0,1\}^*$ is the promise domain and $R\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\times\{0,1\}^*$ is a witness relation. On each $z\in D$, a correct solver must output a binary string $w$ with $(z,w)\in R$. It has no output obligation for $z\notin D$. Unlike a decision task, a search task need not divide its promise into yes and no sets.

For either task, an input encoding and input-length convention are specified separately; correctness is required only for encoded inputs in the declared promise.

For each encoded promised instance $z\in P_n$ of length $n$ (with $P_n$ as in [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]] and its task promise as in [[def-qa-task-and-promise-domain]]), a **query instance** specifies nonnegative integer widths $a(n),b(n)$ and a total function
$$
f_z:\{0,1\}^{a(n)}\to\{0,1\}^{b(n)}.
$$
The promise restricts which $z$ are legal; it does not restrict the address domain of $f_z$. Bit strings label the big-endian computational basis: for a word $x=(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1})$, its slot is $\sum_{k<r}x_k2^{r-1-k}$, with the empty word in slot $0$ ([[def-qc-ordered-bitstring-encoding]]). Ket and bra notation uses the root convention $\langle x|y\rangle_D=\langle y,x\rangle_{\rm root}$ ([[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]]). Its standard quantum query is the coherent XOR oracle from [[def-qc-coherent-function-oracle]], acting on those ordered register bases:
$$
U_{f_z}|x\rangle|y\rangle=|x\rangle|y\oplus f_z(x)\rangle,
$$
where $\oplus$ is coordinatewise addition modulo two, $x$ is an $a(n)$-bit address, and $y$ is a $b(n)$-bit target. One invocation is one query, regardless of the output width. A supplied matrix or a classical description of $f_z$ does not itself supply a circuit decomposition, state preparation, or controlled access at zero cost.

The access contract must specify whether controlled calls are supplied: a controlled call is the explicitly granted block operation $\operatorname{diag}(I,U)$ ([[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]]) and does not follow from an ordinary black-box call. For this standard XOR oracle, $U_{f_z}^{\dagger}=U_{f_z}$ by [[thm-qc-reversible-xor-oracle-unitary]], so an inverse query is the same operation as one ordinary query. Inverse access to any other unitary operation has its own explicitly declared availability and charge ([[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]]). An explicit matrix or classical description supplies no free circuit implementation, preparation, or data loading; those costs are recorded under the declared circuit and gate resource coordinates ([[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]], [[def-qc-elementary-circuit-resources]]).

For $n\ge0$ and $a,x\in\{0,1\}^{n}$, define the one-bit **binary dot product**
$$
a\cdot x:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}(a_i\land x_i),
$$
where $\land$ is Boolean conjunction and $\bigoplus$ is the left-to-right fold of XOR, with empty fold $0$. It is the parity of the number of coordinates where both bits are $1$. Under the quotient operations of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]], this bit represents the sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}[a_i]_2[x_i]_2$ in $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$; the equality uses only the operation definitions, not the field axioms.

citations.quote: Let $f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}$ be the total Boolean function of a [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]. Encode $f$ by its hidden length-two truth table $z=f(0)f(1)\in\{0,1\}^2$, whose associated oracle function is $f_z=f$. The **Deutsch promise** is the decision task with YES set $Y=\{00,11\}$ and NO set $N=\{01,10\}$. The required output is $0$ on $Y$ (constant, $f(0)=f(1)$) and $1$ on $N$ (balanced, $f(0)\ne f(1)$). All four Boolean functions on one bit are promised. The truth table labels the hidden instance; the query interface supplies oracle access to $f$.

A **classical query algorithm** is a finite decision procedure for a fixed encoded instance length $n$ and explicitly declared public data $p$, whose query actions are to the total function $f_z$ of [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]. The procedure is fixed independently of the hidden instance $z$ at fixed $(n,p)$. Its encoding in [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]] labels the instance and determines its size; it does not provide a readable copy of the hidden encoding. Each query chooses an address from $n,p$, earlier replies, and any random bits used so far; it receives the entire $b(n)$-bit reply $f_z(x)$ as one query answer. The address choices may be adaptive. Its terminal output is determined by the same public data, replies, and random tape.

In the ordinary oracle-only model, all dependence on the hidden instance is through these replies. Public parameters such as register widths, a supplied marked count, or an explicit arithmetic input may be used only when the task declares them. A lower bound in the oracle-only model fixes the declared public data across the hidden instances it compares. Additional input-access or preparation capabilities must be explicitly declared with their charges; they are extra resources, not supplied by the hidden instance encoding.

For a randomized algorithm, each branch is determined by the public data, oracle replies, and its finite random tape; the fair-bit tape convention for a bounded-time probabilistic machine is supplied by [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. The query model itself imposes no polynomial bit-time bound. A query bound is a worst-case bound over promised inputs and every random branch; classical computation between queries is charged separately only when a bit-cost model is specified.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

derivations.claim: Fix a deterministic one-query procedure and let $q$ be its queried address. The constant-zero function $f_0$ and the balanced function $g$ defined by $g(q)=0$, $g(1-q)=1$ give the same reply. The procedure therefore has the same transcript and output on two functions requiring different answers, so it cannot be exact.

Querying both addresses reveals the entire truth table; equal replies identify a constant and unequal replies identify a balanced function. Thus two queries suffice exactly, and step 1.1 proves the deterministic exact query complexity is two.

Fix a random tape of an algorithm that makes at most one query. If it makes no query, its one output is correct on at most two of the four truth tables. If it queries address $q$, then for each possible reply $b\in\{0,1\}$ there are exactly two promised functions with $f(q)=b$: one constant and one balanced. The fixed tape gives the same output for both, so it is correct on at most one of each such pair, hence on at most two of the four functions. There are finitely many deterministic one-query strategies on two addresses with binary outputs. The random-tape algorithm induces a probability weight on this finite strategy set by grouping tapes according to their resulting strategy. Averaging the fixed-strategy bound over that finite distribution and over the four functions preserves the bound $1/2$; by [F3] some promised input has success at most $1/2$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of [[def-nat-order]] identified with
membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

derivations.claim: Suppose a deterministic procedure makes at most $N/2$ queries in the worst case. Run it on the constant-zero function and let $S$ be the set of distinct queried addresses. Write $s=|S|\le N/2$ and list the complement $C$ in lexicographic order, with $c=|C|$. Concatenating the lexicographic lists of $S$ and $C$ lists every address exactly once: the sets are disjoint and cover the domain. Indexing this concatenated list gives a bijection from $\{0,\ldots,s+c-1\}$ to the $N$-element address set, so $s+c=N$ by [F3]. Thus $c=N-s\ge N/2$. Choose $T$ to be the first $N/2$ addresses of $C$ and define $g$ to be $1$ on $T$ and $0$ elsewhere. Then $g$ is balanced and agrees with the constant-zero function on every address in $S$. Inductively, each adaptive query and reply in the two executions is the same, so the final outputs agree despite the different correct answers. Thus no such procedure is exact.

Query any fixed set of $N/2+1$ distinct addresses. If all replies are equal, the function cannot be balanced because each value occurs only $N/2$ times in a balanced function, so it is constant. If the replies are not all equal, the function is not constant and is balanced by the promise. This gives an exact procedure using $N/2+1$ queries; combined with step 1.1 the exact complexity is $N/2+1$.

citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$, let $N:=2^n$, and let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ be the total function of a [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]. The **Deutsch–Jozsa promise** is the decision task with YES set consisting of constant functions and NO set consisting of functions taking each value $0$ and $1$ exactly $N/2$ times. The required output is constant or balanced, respectively. Here $n$ is the address width, and $N$ is the number of addresses, as supplied by [[thm-qc-bitstring-index-is-bijection]] and [[def-finite-cardinality]]. Encode an instance by its $N$-bit truth table in lexicographic address order; its encoded input size is therefore $N$, not $n$, under [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]]. In the query-instance convention, the length-$N$ family has address width $a(N)=n$ and reply width $b(N)=1$; the public parameter $n$ determines the registers, while the unknown truth table is supplied through oracle queries. Lengths that are not powers of two at least two have empty promise.

A **classical query algorithm** is a finite decision procedure for a fixed encoded instance length $n$ and explicitly declared public data $p$, whose query actions are to the total function $f_z$ of [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]. The procedure is fixed independently of the hidden instance $z$ at fixed $(n,p)$. Its encoding in [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]] labels the instance and determines its size; it does not provide a readable copy of the hidden encoding. Each query chooses an address from $n,p$, earlier replies, and any random bits used so far; it receives the entire $b(n)$-bit reply $f_z(x)$ as one query answer. The address choices may be adaptive. Its terminal output is determined by the same public data, replies, and random tape.

In the ordinary oracle-only model, all dependence on the hidden instance is through these replies. Public parameters such as register widths, a supplied marked count, or an explicit arithmetic input may be used only when the task declares them. A lower bound in the oracle-only model fixes the declared public data across the hidden instances it compares. Additional input-access or preparation capabilities must be explicitly declared with their charges; they are extra resources, not supplied by the hidden instance encoding.

For a randomized algorithm, each branch is determined by the public data, oracle replies, and its finite random tape; the fair-bit tape convention for a bounded-time probabilistic machine is supplied by [[def-probabilistic-polynomial-time-machine-interface]]. The query model itself imposes no polynomial bit-time bound. A query bound is a worst-case bound over promised inputs and every random branch; classical computation between queries is charged separately only when a bit-cost model is specified.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{N}$ is the set of von Neumann naturals
([[def-natural-numbers]]): $0 = \varnothing$, $\sigma(n) = n \cup \{n\}$, and
$n = \{\, m \in \mathbb{N} : m < n \,\}$ is itself the set of its predecessors,
the order being the additive order of [[def-nat-order]] identified with
membership in [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]. Write $A \approx B$ when a
bijection $A \to B$ exists ([[def-equinumerous]],
[[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). A set $A$ is **finite** when
$A \approx n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-countable]]).

**Definition.** Let $A$ be a finite set. Then there is **exactly one**
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $A \approx n$, and we write

$$\lvert A\rvert := \text{that } n,$$

the **cardinality**, or number of elements, of $A$. The notation $\lvert A\rvert$
is defined for finite $A$ only, and its value is a natural number.

**Why exactly one, which is the whole content of the definition.** At least one
such $n$ exists: that is literally what "$A$ is finite" says. At most one exists:
if $A \approx n$ and $A \approx m$ with $n, m \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \approx A$,
because the inverse of a bijection is a bijection, and hence $n \approx m$,
because a composition of bijections is a bijection
([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]); and $n \approx m$ forces $n = m$ by
claim 3 of [[lem-pigeonhole]]. So $\lvert A\rvert$ names a single natural number
and not a family of choices.

**Four consequences, proved here because everything on this page uses them.**

**(a) $\lvert n\rvert = n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.** The identity map
$\mathrm{id}_n$ is a bijection $n \to n$, so $n \approx n$; thus $n$ is finite and
the unique natural equinumerous with it is $n$ itself.

**(b) $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$, and a finite $A$ satisfies
$\lvert A\rvert = 0$ if and only if $A = \varnothing$.** Since $0 = \varnothing$,
part (a) gives $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$. Conversely, if $\lvert A\rvert = 0$
then there is a bijection $f : A \to \varnothing$; were some $a \in A$, the value
$f(a)$ would be an element of $\varnothing$, and $\varnothing$ has none, so
$A = \varnothing$.

**(c) Transport along a bijection.** If $A$ is finite and $f : A \to B$ is a
bijection, then $B$ is finite and $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$. Indeed
$B \approx A$ through $f^{-1}$ and $A \approx \lvert A\rvert$, so
$B \approx \lvert A\rvert$ by transitivity.

**(d) Equality of cardinalities is equinumerosity.** For finite $A$ and $B$:
$\lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert$ if and only if $A \approx B$. If the
cardinalities agree then $A \approx \lvert A\rvert = \lvert B\rvert \approx B$;
conversely $A \approx B$ gives $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ by (c).

derivations.claim: For a constant function, all three replies agree, so the procedure outputs constant correctly with probability one. For a balanced function write $m=N/2$. The ordered sample space has $N(N-1)(N-2)$ triples. If $m=2$, no three distinct samples can have the same reply, so the error probability is zero. If $m\ge3$, the error event consists of an ordered triple all drawn from the zero class or all from the one class; its probability is $\frac{2m(m-1)(m-2)}{(2m)(2m-1)(2m-2)}=\frac{m-2}{2(2m-1)}=\frac{N-4}{4(N-1)}.$ This is at most $1/4$, since $N-4\le N-1$.

The without-replacement experiment has success at least $3/4$ by step 1.1. For an implementation in the finite fair-bit model, take three independent blocks of $n$ fair bits as addresses, allowing repetitions. On a balanced input the three replies are independent fair bits, so they all agree with probability $2(1/2)^3=1/4$; on a constant input they always agree. Thus this algorithm uses exactly $3n$ random bits and three value queries and has success at least $3/4$. When $n=1$, the domain has two addresses and querying both returns the full truth table, which classifies exactly. The claim concerns bounded-error upper cost and leaves the deterministic exact lower bound as a separate query measure.

derivations.claim: Fix a random tape. The algorithm is a deterministic adaptive binary decision tree of depth at most $q$, since each query reply is one bit by [F2]. A binary tree of depth at most $q$ has at most $2^q$ leaves: this holds at depth zero, and at each added level every prior leaf creates at most two children. Each leaf outputs one candidate secret, so at most one of the $2^n$ secrets reaching that leaf can be correctly recovered. Hence success averaged uniformly over secrets is at most $2^q/2^n=2^{q-n}$.

For fixed $n$ and $q$, there are finitely many deterministic depth-at-most-$q$ decision trees on the finite address set, with output labels in $\{0,1\}^n$. The random-tape algorithm induces weights on this finite strategy set by grouping tapes according to their tree. Averaging step 1.1 over this finite distribution leaves average success at most $2^{q-n}$. If worst-case success is at least $2/3$ on every secret, its average under the uniform secret law is at least $2/3$. For $q\le n-1$, the upper bound is at most $1/2<2/3$, a contradiction; therefore $q\ge n$.
For each coordinate $i<n$, query $e_i$, the string with one at $i$ and zeros elsewhere. By [F2], the reply is $f_a(e_i)=a_i$. These $n$ replies give the entire secret, so $n$ queries suffice exactly.

**Input.** A one-bit total Boolean oracle $f$ satisfying the Deutsch promise of [[def-qa-deutsch-promise]], with an address qubit $A$ and target qubit $T$ initialized to $|0\rangle_A|0\rangle_T$.

**Output.** One classical bit: output $0$ for constant and $1$ for balanced.

**Gate model.** The declared nonoracle gate alphabet permits exact callable $H$ and $X$ gates, each occurrence charged as one nonoracle gate under [[def-qa-nonoracle-gate-cost]]. The supplied standard bit query is charged separately as one oracle call.

**Procedure.** Apply $X$ to $T$, then apply $H$ to $T$ and $H$ to $A$. Invoke the standard XOR oracle $U_f$ once on the ordered pair $(A,T)$. Apply $H$ to $A$, measure $A$ in its ordered computational basis, and output the measured bit. There are no intermediate measurements, loops, or failure branches.

The terminal measurement is specified by [[def-qa-finite-branch-output-law]] and is separate from the declared one-qubit gate resource. No circuit-uniformity or classical bit-time bound is asserted.

The standard bit query and its controlled-access conventions are those of [[def-qa-standard-bit-query]] and [[def-qa-quantum-query-algorithm]]. The one-query phase action used by this procedure is verified by [[thm-qa-bit-query-to-phase-query]].

Let $f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}$ be the total Boolean function of a [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]. Encode $f$ by its hidden length-two truth table $z=f(0)f(1)\in\{0,1\}^2$, whose associated oracle function is $f_z=f$. The **Deutsch promise** is the decision task with YES set $Y=\{00,11\}$ and NO set $N=\{01,10\}$. The required output is $0$ on $Y$ (constant, $f(0)=f(1)$) and $1$ on $N$ (balanced, $f(0)\ne f(1)$). All four Boolean functions on one bit are promised. The truth table labels the hidden instance; the query interface supplies oracle access to $f$.

Let $f:\{0,1\}^{a}\to\{0,1\}$ be total. Starting a target qubit in $|0\rangle$, apply $X$ and then $H$, and make one standard bit query. Since $HX|0\rangle=|-\rangle$, phase kickback implements $P_f$ on the address and returns the target to $|-\rangle$. This conversion uses one query plus exactly two nonoracle one-qubit gates; the target preparation is explicit and assumes no preprepared state or generic amplitude loading.

In the computational basis $(|0\rangle,|1\rangle)$, use $X,Y,Z$ from [[def-qc-pauli-matrices]] and define
$$H:=\frac{X+Z}{\sqrt2}=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad S:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&i\end{pmatrix},\qquad T:=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix}.$$
The phases displayed in these matrices are exact; they are not identified modulo a scalar when the matrices are later placed under a control.

For real $\theta$ and a real unit vector $\mathbf n=(n_x,n_y,n_z)$, define the axis rotation
$$R_{\mathbf n}(\theta):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{i\theta}{2}\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\right),\qquad R_z(\theta):=R_{(0,0,1)}(\theta).$$
Here $\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}$ and $\|\mathbf n\|_2$ have the meanings fixed in [[def-qc-bloch-coordinate-map]]. For a bounded endomorphism $B$ of $Q_2$, the notation $\exp(B)$ means the operator-norm series $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}B^k/k!$ of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]] at scalar parameter $1$. Its convergence applies here because $Q_2$ is finite-dimensional and complete and every linear endomorphism of $Q_2$ is bounded ([[cor-finite-dimensional-normed-spaces-are-banach]], [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]).

The unitary identities for the fixed matrices are verified below. The following theorem proves the closed form and unitarity of each $R_{\mathbf n}(\theta)$.

Fix an encoded input $x$ and a finite rooted execution tree on the same declared finite register $H_n$ at every node. Its root state is the density operator of the standard input basis state with zero-initialized work registers. Every nonterminal node is either a unitary endomorphism $U:H_n\to H_n$ or a finite instrument $(\mathcal I_a)_{a\in\Omega_h}$ whose branch maps are from $\mathcal L(H_n)$ to $\mathcal L(H_n)$. The observed outcome label $a$ is retained for classical feed-forward, while a hidden Kraus label is not a branch. The tree has finite depth and finite outcome sets.

Every nonterminal node is either a unitary endomorphism $U:H_n\to H_n$ or a finite instrument $(\mathcal I_a)_{a\in\Omega_h}$ whose branch maps are from $\mathcal L(H_n)$ to $\mathcal L(H_n)$. The observed outcome label $a$ is retained for classical feed-forward, while a hidden Kraus label is not a branch. The tree has finite depth and finite outcome sets.

Assign the root weight $w(\varnothing)=1$. At a unitary edge set $\rho_{h'}=U\rho_hU^\dagger$ and $w(h')=w(h)$. At an instrument node set $q_{h,a}=\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal I_a(\rho_h))$ and $w(ha)=w(h)q_{h,a}$. If $q_{h,a}>0$, set $\rho_{ha}=\mathcal I_a(\rho_h)/q_{h,a}$; if $q_{h,a}=0$, that child and its descendants have weight zero and contribute no state or output weight. The instrument and conditional-state conventions are those of [[def-qc-instrument-and-conditional-state]].

At each positive-weight leaf $\ell$, the ordered output wires have a fixed length $m$ and are disjoint from the remaining wires $W_\ell$. For $z\in\{0,1\}^m$ and a bit string $v$ on $W_\ell$, let $e_{\ell,z,v}$ be the full-register computational-basis vector with those bits in their declared wire positions. Define the leaf output weight and total output law by
$$q_\ell(z):=\sum_{v\in\{0,1\}^{|W_\ell|}}\langle \rho_\ell e_{\ell,z,v},e_{\ell,z,v}\rangle_{\rm root},\qquad P(z\mid x):=\sum_{\ell\text{ positive-weight leaf}}w(\ell)q_\ell(z).$$
The classical output predicate $A_n(x,z)$ selects the acceptance event by summing $P(z\mid x)$ over the finite set of accepted strings. This definition extends the terminal-output convention of [[def-qc-promise-computation-model]] to finite instrument branches; the verification proves that $P(\cdot\mid x)$ is a normalized probability law and every acceptance probability lies in $[0,1]$.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in its first argument, and let $u\in H$ satisfy $\|u\|=1$. Define $P_u:=|u\rangle\langle u|$ by the root-linear-first Dirac convention. Then $P_u$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, has one-dimensional range, is non-negative, and has trace one. In particular, $P_u$ is a density operator.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

citations.quote: Let $f:\{0,1\}\to\{0,1\}$ be the total Boolean function of a [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]. Encode $f$ by its hidden length-two truth table $z=f(0)f(1)\in\{0,1\}^2$, whose associated oracle function is $f_z=f$. The **Deutsch promise** is the decision task with YES set $Y=\{00,11\}$ and NO set $N=\{01,10\}$. The required output is $0$ on $Y$ (constant, $f(0)=f(1)$) and $1$ on $N$ (balanced, $f(0)\ne f(1)$). All four Boolean functions on one bit are promised. The truth table labels the hidden instance; the query interface supplies oracle access to $f$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $N:=2^n$, and let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ be the total function of a [[def-qa-promise-query-instance]]. The **Deutsch–Jozsa promise** is the decision task with YES set consisting of constant functions and NO set consisting of functions taking each value $0$ and $1$ exactly $N/2$ times. The required output is constant or balanced, respectively. Here $n$ is the address width, and $N$ is the number of addresses, as supplied by [[thm-qc-bitstring-index-is-bijection]] and [[def-finite-cardinality]]. Encode an instance by its $N$-bit truth table in lexicographic address order; its encoded input size is therefore $N$, not $n$, under [[def-qa-input-encoding-and-size]]. In the query-instance convention, the length-$N$ family has address width $a(N)=n$ and reply width $b(N)=1$; the public parameter $n$ determines the registers, while the unknown truth table is supplied through oracle queries. Lengths that are not powers of two at least two have empty promise.

Let $n\ge1$. The **Bernstein–Vazirani no-offset promise** consists of the total functions
$$
f_a:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\qquad f_a(x):=a\cdot x,
$$
for an unknown secret $a\in\{0,1\}^n$, using [[def-qa-binary-dot-product]]. The task is to output $a$. This version has no additive offset: the oracle is exactly $f_a$, not $x\mapsto a\cdot x\oplus b$.

For $n\ge0$ and $a,x\in\{0,1\}^{n}$, define the one-bit **binary dot product**
$$
a\cdot x:=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{n-1}(a_i\land x_i),
$$
where $\land$ is Boolean conjunction and $\bigoplus$ is the left-to-right fold of XOR, with empty fold $0$. It is the parity of the number of coordinates where both bits are $1$. Under the quotient operations of [[def-qa-binary-field-f2]], this bit represents the sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}[a_i]_2[x_i]_2$ in $\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$; the equality uses only the operation definitions, not the field axioms.

For either promised one-bit function $f$, the final measurement of [[alg-qa-deutsch-query]] outputs $0$ with probability one when $f$ is constant and $1$ with probability one when $f$ is balanced. In the algorithm's declared exact $X,H$ gate model, it uses exactly one oracle query and one $X$ and three $H$ gates, totaling four one-qubit gates. The terminal measurement is a separate resource.

For every $n\ge1$ and every function satisfying the Deutsch–Jozsa promise, [[alg-qa-deutsch-jozsa-query]] outputs constant with probability one on constant inputs and balanced with probability one on balanced inputs. In the algorithm's declared exact $X,H$ gate model, it uses exactly one oracle query and one $X$ and $2n+1$ $H$ gates, totaling $2n+2$ one-qubit gates. The terminal measurement is a separate resource.

For every $n\ge1$ and every no-offset Bernstein–Vazirani function $f_a(x)=a\cdot x$, [[alg-qa-bernstein-vazirani-query]] outputs the secret $a$ with probability one. In the algorithm's declared exact $X,H$ gate model, it uses exactly one oracle query and one $X$ and $2n+1$ $H$ gates, totaling $2n+2$ one-qubit gates. The terminal measurement is a separate resource.

On the Deutsch promise, the exact deterministic classical query complexity is $2$. Every randomized classical algorithm making at most one query has worst-case success probability at most $1/2$ under per-input correctness.
For $n\ge1$ and $N=2^n$, the exact deterministic classical query complexity of the Deutsch–Jozsa promise is $N/2+1$.

For $n\ge2$, the finite probability experiment that samples three distinct addresses uniformly without replacement and outputs constant exactly when all three replies agree has success probability at least $3/4$ on every Deutsch–Jozsa input. In the finite fair-bit classical query model, sampling three independent uniform addresses with replacement and using the same output rule also succeeds with probability at least $3/4$, using exactly $3n$ random bits and three value queries. For $n=1$, querying both addresses solves the promise exactly with two queries. Thus the deterministic exact lower bound is not a bounded-error exponential separation.

For the no-offset Bernstein–Vazirani promise on $n\ge1$ bits, every randomized classical algorithm with worst-case success at least $2/3$ needs at least $n$ queries. Querying the $n$ standard basis addresses recovers the secret exactly, so the bounded-error and exact classical query complexities are both $n$.

For $n\ge1$ and $z\in\{0,1\}^n$, with the binary dot product of [[def-qa-binary-dot-product]],
$$
\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}(-1)^{x\cdot z}=\begin{cases}2^n,&z=0^n,\\0,&z\ne0^n.\end{cases}
$$
Consequently, for every $x\in\{0,1\}^n$,
$$
H^{\otimes n}|x\rangle=2^{-n/2}\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^n}(-1)^{x\cdot y}|y\rangle,
$$
where $H$ is the exact one-qubit gate of [[def-qc-one-qubit-gate-alphabet-and-rotations]] and tensor factors follow the ordered register convention of [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]].

derivations.claim: The Deutsch truth tables give $(f(0),f(1))=00,11\Longrightarrow\text{constant},\qquad (f(0),f(1))=01,10\Longrightarrow\text{balanced}.$ The exact Deutsch theorem [F4] therefore outputs $0$ on the first two tables and $1$ on the latter two.

For the two-bit Deutsch–Jozsa function $f(x)=x_0$, the table is $00\mapsto0$, $01\mapsto0$, $10\mapsto1$, $11\mapsto1$, so it is balanced by [F2]. Its final address amplitude is $\alpha_y=\frac14\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^2}(-1)^{x_0+x\cdot y}.$ For $y=00,01,10,11$, these sums are respectively $0,0,4,0$, so the measured output is $10$. The classical exact bound is $N/2+1=3$ queries, and the three-distinct-sample experiment is exact for $N=4$ because any three of four addresses include both output values.

For $a=10$, the two-bit Bernstein–Vazirani amplitude at $y$ is $\alpha_y=\frac14\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^2}(-1)^{x\cdot(10\oplus y)}.$ The sums for $y=00,01,10,11$ are $0,0,4,0$, respectively; hence the exact output is $10$. By [F5], classical bounded-error recovery needs at least two queries and the two basis queries suffice.

For Deutsch, the deterministic exact classical query count is two while one randomized query has worst-case success at most $1/2$ by [F5]. For two-bit Deutsch–Jozsa the exact deterministic count is three, while the without-replacement three-sample experiment succeeds with probability one on this finite domain. The finite fair-bit algorithm with replacement has success at least $3/4$ by [F5]. For two-bit Bernstein–Vazirani two classical queries recover both secret bits. These are query counts; none is a classical bit-time claim.
